appraisal_events.evidence: "il ne se suffisait plus à lui-même, il n'était plus que l'intermédiaire nécessaire entre ces jeunes filles et moi ; le prestige que, quelques instants encore auparavant, lui donnait pour moi son talent, ne valait plus qu'en tant qu'il m'en conférait un peu à moi-même aux yeux de la petite bande"; the narrator paces, invents a thousand pretexts, and glosses his own patience as "signe avant-coureur du pernicieux amour-propre" springing from "mon total égoïsme".
appraisal_events.explanation: The painter's worth collapses into pure instrumentality the moment the girl passes the window; the narration presents that collapse as a symptom of the watcher's desire and vanity rather than as a judgment on Elstir.

appraisal_events.evidence: Asked what became of the model, "Un étonnement provoqué par mes paroles précéda sur la figure d'Elstir l'air indifférent et distrait qu'au bout d'une seconde il y étendit"; he hurries the watercolour out of sight — "j'entends Madame Elstir qui arrive et bien que la jeune personne au melon n'ait joué, je vous assure, aucun rôle dans ma vie, il est inutile que ma femme ait cette aquarelle sous les yeux" — then disparages his own work, "les mains sont d'un commençant".
appraisal_events.explanation: A single question puts him visibly off balance in front of a guest: he masks his surprise, volunteers an unasked denial, and hides the picture from his wife.

appraisal_events.evidence: First "Je la trouvai très ennuyeuse", greying, "commune sans être simple"; but Elstir says "Ma belle Gabrielle !" with "une douceur respectueuse", and once the narrator knows his mythological painting "Mme Elstir prit pour moi aussi de la beauté" — the incarnation of the canon he has given his whole life to, so that "son corps perdit de sa lourdeur" and she becomes "une créature immatérielle, un portrait d'Elstir".
appraisal_events.explanation: The passage first records a flat dismissal and then reverses it: through her husband's cult she is raised from dull provincial matron to the realized form of his ideal of Beauty.

appraisal_events.evidence: The narrator's questions on the digue are ruses "pour faire demeurer Elstir à l'endroit où je croyais que ces jeunes filles pouvaient encore passer", and he concedes that the novelty of the "Port de Carquethuit" "tenait peut-être plus à la vision du peintre qu'à un mérite spécial de cette plage"; Elstir answers with a connoisseur's authority — "Ici, la ligne de la plage est quelconque ; mais là-bas, je ne peux vous dire quelle grâce elle a, quelle douceur."
appraisal_events.explanation: In the closing exchange the painter holds the discourse and is credited with making the coast worth seeing, while his companion's talk is nothing but pretext.

status_effects.explanation: Within the scene his standing drops from admired master to necessary go-between, valued only for the introduction he can perform.
The same passage turns the judgment back on him: he confesses total egoism, unavowed self-love, and shame at motives that are 'point à mon honneur'.
He loses composure for a second, has to compose a face and an excuse, and is shown managing what his wife must not see.
Dismissed as dull and common on sight, she ends the passage endowed with an almost divine value as the living form of her husband's ideal.
On the digue he speaks with unchallenged authority about the coast and corrects the premise of the question, while the narrator's own words are hollow manoeuvres.

ambiguities: The watercolour's model is identified only by the inscription 'Miss Sacripant, octobre 1872' and the narrator explicitly does not know who she is; resolving her to Odette rests on the reference sheet's alias, not on anything the passage states, so no status movement is recorded for her.
